cues.text: Welcome to Biomolecules.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Carbohydrates include sugars and their larger assemblies.
Monosaccharides cannot be hydrolysed into simpler carbohydrate units.
An aldose has an aldehyde group in its open chain representation; a ketose has
a ketone.
Glucose is an aldohexose and fructose a ketohexose: both have six carbons, but
their carbonyl positions differ.
Many sugars spend most of their time in cyclic forms in solution, so an open
chain formula is a useful representation rather than the only structure
present.
Ring formation creates an anomeric centre.
Do not identify a carbohydrate solely from the often used simple carbon and
water composition pattern; some compounds fit it without being carbohydrates
and some carbohydrate derivatives do not fit it.
For glucose and fructose, six carbon atoms and the same overall composition do
not imply the same functional group position.
Classification combines the carbon count with the open chain carbonyl type.
Ring drawings add a further distinction between alpha and beta forms at an
anomeric centre.
A formula comparison should therefore be followed by a connectivity check
before naming a sugar.
Sucrose contains glucose and fructose units.
Maltose contains two glucose units, while lactose contains galactose and
glucose.
Joining two monosaccharides with a glycosidic bond has the net composition
change of losing one water molecule; hydrolysis adds water and separates the
units.
Structural bonding details distinguish the three despite related overall
formulas.
A reducing sugar can access a reactive carbonyl form under the relevant test
conditions.
Sucrose has both anomeric centres involved in its linkage and is nonreducing
before hydrolysis.
Maltose and lactose retain a suitable free anomeric centre and are reducing.
Fructose can respond in alkaline reducing sugar tests through rearrangement
even though it is a ketose.
For one mole of sucrose hydrolysed completely, one mole each of glucose and
fructose appears.
One mole of maltose gives two moles of glucose instead.
The total monosaccharide amount doubles, while the carbon inventory is
conserved.
Water participates in hydrolysis, so adding the masses of the isolated sugar
units need not equal the original dry disaccharide mass alone.
Starch and glycogen store glucose units, whereas cellulose has a structural
role.
Different linkage arrangements change properties even when the repeating
monosaccharide is glucose.
This is an example of why a monomer name alone cannot specify the behaviour of
a polymer.
The official Chemistry unit emphasizes the named monosaccharides and the
constituent units of sucrose, maltose and lactose.
Use larger polysaccharides as supporting context rather than claiming every
biological polymer detail is required.
For a hydrolysis question, track the type and number of released units, not
simply whether the original substance has a sweet taste.
Amylose is largely unbranched, while amylopectin and glycogen have branching.
Cellulose uses a different glucose linkage arrangement that gives extended
structural chains.
Humans do not digest cellulose with the same enzymes used for starch.
These contrasts connect molecular bonding with macroscopic properties without
changing the identity of the glucose building block.
Linkage and branching must accompany the monomer name in a comparison.
A typical alpha amino acid has amino and carboxyl groups associated with the
same alpha carbon.
Its side chain distinguishes it from other amino acids.
In suitable aqueous conditions, it can exist as a zwitterion carrying both
positive and negative charges; the dominant ionic form depends on p H and the
side chain.
A peptide bond is the amide linkage with a carbonyl carbon bonded to nitrogen
formed between amino acid residues.
The net assembly of a simple linear chain of n amino acids forms n minus one
peptide links and releases n minus one waters in a condensation bookkeeping
model.
Living synthesis is more elaborate than directly mixing free amino acids.
Hydrolysis breaks the links and adds water.
For five amino acid residues in one noncyclic linear chain, four joins are
needed.
That gives four peptide bonds and four net water losses in the simple
bookkeeping model.
A cyclic peptide or several separate chains would require different counting.
Glycine has two hydrogens at its alpha carbon, unlike a typical amino acid
with
four distinct attached groups, so do not automatically assign every amino acid
a stereogenic alpha carbon.
Protein structure is described at four different levels.
Primary structure gives the amino acid sequence along a polypeptide chain.
Secondary structure describes recurring local backbone arrangements, including
alpha helices and beta sheets, with hydrogen bonds playing an important
stabilizing role.
Tertiary structure is the complete three dimensional folding of one chain.
Quaternary structure describes how several polypeptide subunits are arranged
together.
A single chain protein can have the first three levels without having
quaternary structure.
Keep the sequence separate from the way that sequence folds.
Denaturation changes the folded organization and can reduce biological
activity.
It does not necessarily break peptide bonds or turn the whole protein into
free
amino acids.
Heat and changes in chemical environment can disturb stabilizing interactions,
but different proteins respond differently.
Refolding is not guaranteed simply by restoring the original temperature.
In a comparison question, identify whether the evidence concerns sequence,
local backbone folding, the shape of one complete chain or the association of
several chains.
Loss of activity with an intact peptide backbone supports a folding change
rather than complete hydrolysis.
Enzymes are biological catalysts; most are proteins, though some catalytic RNA
molecules also exist.
A suitable active site helps bind substrates and provide a lower barrier
pathway.
Specificity reflects structure and interactions, not an absolute promise that
one enzyme acts on only one possible molecule.
Like other catalysts, enzymes do not change the equilibrium constant for a
reaction at the same conditions.
Activity depends on factors such as temperature and p H, and extreme
conditions
can damage structure.
More heat does not mean unlimited acceleration because the catalyst can lose
its working form.
An enzyme changes the barrier along a reaction pathway and can accelerate both
directions toward equilibrium.
It does not force a different final equilibrium composition merely by being a
catalyst.
Changing acidity or temperature can change both the chemical environment and
the enzyme structure.
Compare activity measurements only when the substrate amount, conditions and
measured interval are appropriately controlled.
Vitamins are needed in small amounts for normal biochemical functions.
The usual classification places A, D, E and K among fat soluble vitamins
and the B group and C among water soluble vitamins.
These are families with distinct roles, not one interchangeable chemical.
Hormones are chemical signals acting through suitable biological targets; some
are peptides, some steroids and others have different structures.
Insulin is a peptide hormone example, whereas many steroid hormones derive
from
a different molecular framework.
Vitamin classification and hormone classification answer different questions.
Solubility places vitamins into broad groups; it does not state a universal
molecular structure or biochemical role.
A peptide hormone has amino acid residues joined in a chain, while a steroid
hormone has a different carbon framework.
Recognize insulin as a peptide example and keep the two classification systems
separate during revision.
Recognizing a family name does not uniquely determine every reaction or
functional group.
Compare the actual molecular framework when a structure is supplied rather
than
treating all biological signalling compounds as the same class.
A nucleoside combines a nitrogenous base and a sugar.
Adding a phosphate component gives a nucleotide, the building block of nucleic
acids.
DNA uses deoxyribose and typically the bases A, G, C and T; RNA uses
ribose and usually A, G, C and U.
The sugar phosphate backbone joins units through phosphodiester links.
In the elementary double stranded DNA model, A pairs with T and G with C, with
complementary antiparallel strands.
DNA stores hereditary information, while RNA has roles in expressing and
processing it.
Complementary DNA base count rules apply to a whole double stranded sample; do
not impose equal A and T on an arbitrary single RNA strand.
If adenine accounts for thirty percent of a whole complementary double
stranded
DNA sample, thymine is also thirty percent.
Forty percent remains for guanine plus cytosine, giving twenty percent each.
This calculation uses complementarity over both strands.
A single isolated strand can have unequal adenine and thymine counts, and RNA
substitutes uracil for thymine in the usual elementary comparison.
A Fischer projection encodes stereochemistry and is not simply a vertical
decorative formula.
For open chain D glucose, place the aldehyde group at the top and the terminal
hydroxymethyl group at the bottom.
The hydroxyl positions from carbon two through carbon five are right, left,
right and right.
Horizontal bonds point toward the viewer and vertical bonds point away in this
projection convention.
Carbon one belongs to the aldehyde; carbon six belongs to the terminal
hydroxymethyl group.
The D label is assigned by the configuration at the highest numbered
stereogenic centre in this standard comparison, which is carbon five here.
It does not mean every hydroxyl lies on the right.
Nor does D automatically predict positive optical rotation.
Changing one stereogenic centre can give a different sugar; merely rotating a
whole spatial molecule does not.
The projection is a useful open chain representation even though aqueous
glucose is mainly cyclic.
Keep carbon numbering visible when connecting the chain to a ring so that the
anomeric carbon can be identified correctly.
When glucose forms a six membered pyranose ring, the carbon five hydroxyl
oxygen connects with the carbon one aldehyde carbon to make a cyclic
hemiacetal.
Carbon one becomes the anomeric centre.
Two configurations are possible there while the other stereogenic centres
retain their relationships.
In the standard Haworth representation of D glucopyranose with the
hydroxymethyl group drawn up, an anomeric hydroxyl drawn down is alpha and one
drawn up is beta.
More generally, compare the anomeric hydroxyl with the reference hydroxymethyl
group: trans gives alpha and cis gives beta for this representation.
The schematic highlights those groups and does not show every hydroxyl.
The two anomers can interconvert through ring opening and closure in solution,
producing mutarotation.
They are not different molecular formulas and they are not simply two
conformations of one unchanged anomeric configuration.
Alpha and beta labels also do not mean the signs of optical rotation.
A chair conformation supplies further three dimensional information beyond
this
simplified ring projection, which should not be treated as an exact planar
molecular shape.
A free anomeric hemiacetal can open to a carbonyl form and provides a useful
way to identify a reducing end.
Maltose and lactose retain a free anomeric centre and are reducing
disaccharides in the usual comparison.
Sucrose links the anomeric centres of its glucose and fructose units, so it
lacks that free reducing end before hydrolysis.
Its hydrolysis gives one mole of glucose and one mole of fructose per mole of
sucrose.
With rounded molar masses, three hundred forty two grams of sucrose reacts
with
eighteen grams of water to give one hundred eighty grams of each
monosaccharide.
The total product mass is three hundred sixty grams; water has become part of
the products rather than mass appearing from nowhere.
Fructose can give reducing test behaviour under suitable alkaline conditions
despite its open chain ketone classification, so aldehyde naming alone is not
the complete criterion.
Distinguish a sugar before hydrolysis from the mixture produced afterward.
A change in a test result can reveal a changed linkage or newly accessible
reducing end.
An amino acid contains groups that can gain or lose protons, so its
predominant
charge depends on p H.
Glycine provides a simple example without an ionizable side chain.
In sufficiently acidic solution, its amino group is protonated and its
carboxyl
group is mostly neutral, giving net charge plus one.
In the intermediate zwitterionic form, the amino group remains positive while
the carboxylate is negative, giving net charge zero.
In sufficiently basic solution, the carboxylate remains negative and the amino
group is neutral, giving net charge minus one.
A zwitterion is therefore not a structure with no formal charges; it has
opposite charges in the same molecule.
At the isoelectric point, the average net charge is zero under the stated
conditions.
This does not mean every molecule has permanently lost both acid base
functions.
Amino acids with ionizable side chains need additional protonation states and
cannot be analysed by copying glycine's pattern alone.
Identify all ionizable groups, compare the p H with the relevant dissociation
constants, and then add their charges.
A peptide bond joins a carboxyl carbon of one amino acid to the nitrogen of
another, with loss of water in the simplified condensation account.
A linear chain with five residues has four peptide links and loses four water
molecules when assembled from those free amino acids.
A cyclic chain has different end group bookkeeping, so the linear rule must be
stated.
Sequence is directional: glycine followed by alanine is not the same
connectivity as alanine followed by glycine, although the two dipeptides have
the same total composition.
Write from the amino terminus to the carboxyl terminus in the usual sequence
convention.
Using illustrative rounded molar masses of seventy five for glycine and eighty
nine for alanine, forming one dipeptide gives seventy five plus eighty nine
minus eighteen, or one hundred forty six grams per mole.
Hydrolysis reverses the water balance.
This calculation concerns one condensation link, not the loss of an entire
hydroxyl or amino group from the residue count.
Distinguish sequence, number of residues, number of links and mass balance
before comparing peptide formulas.
